questions.q: Why should you determine whether a failure is "cannot connect" vs. "login failed" before touching any firewall rule?
options: Because "login failed" means the network layer already succeeded and the real cause is in Chapter 4's territory (auth), not this chapter's network layer — checking the wrong layer first wastes time
Because firewall rules can only be checked after a successful login
Because login failures are always caused by NSG misconfiguration
There's no reason — both symptoms always share the same root cause
questions.explain: A login failure means the packet already got through the network layer; debugging firewalls at that point is the wrong layer entirely.

questions.q: What is a common mistake when checking firewall rules during troubleshooting?
options: Assuming a client's IP instead of confirming its actual current public IP, which can change due to dynamic ISP assignment, VPN egress, or corporate NAT
Running SELECT * FROM sys.firewall_rules against the wrong server entirely
Firewall rules never need to be checked when troubleshooting connectivity
Checking database-level rules is never necessary, only server-level
questions.explain: Client IPs change more often than expected — the Portal's connection error often shows the actual IP it saw, which is the fastest way to confirm this.

questions.q: Why can an NSG block a connection even when the VNet service endpoint and Virtual Network rule are both configured correctly?
options: Because NSGs are evaluated independently of Azure SQL's own firewall layer and can block outbound traffic on the required port regardless of Azure SQL-side configuration
NSGs cannot block Azure SQL traffic under any configuration
NSGs only affect Managed Instance, never Azure SQL Database
Because NSGs replace the need for a Virtual Network rule entirely
questions.explain: NSGs sit at a different layer and must be checked separately from the service endpoint and VNet rule configuration.

questions.q: When troubleshooting a Private Endpoint connection, what does an nslookup resolving to a PUBLIC IP (instead of private) from inside the VNet indicate?
options: The Private DNS zone (privatelink.database.windows.net) either isn't linked to that VNet, or a record is missing/stale
The connection is working correctly and no further action is needed
TLS is misconfigured on the client
The firewall rule for that IP range needs to be removed
questions.explain: This is one of the most common real-world Private Link failure points, per Lesson 28 and confirmed here as part of the troubleshooting order.

questions.q: Why does a TLS version mismatch often look like a "connects, then dies" symptom rather than an obvious firewall block?
options: Because the TLS handshake happens AFTER the network path (firewall/VNet/DNS) already succeeded, so the failure surfaces at a later stage than a network-layer rejection
Because TLS mismatches are actually firewall issues in disguise
Because TLS is checked before DNS resolution in every case
TLS version has no effect on connection behavior
questions.explain: This is exactly why the troubleshooting checklist orders TLS last among the network-related checks — it only matters once earlier layers already passed.
